title: Percent in money: discounts, profit and loss
summary: Use a 100% bar to see how much a discount takes off a price, and what percentage of the cost a seller gains or loses.
guide: In each problem the whole bar is 100%: the original price or the cost. With 10 parts each part is 10%; with 4 parts, 25%; with 5 parts, 20%.
A {{term:discount}} is the amount taken off the {{term:price}}. 20% off means you pay 80% of the price.
A seller buys something (the cost) and sells it. Selling for more makes a {{term:profit}}; selling for less makes a {{term:loss}}. The percentage profit or loss is always worked out from the cost.
This is not in the Key Stage 2 curriculum: it is extra, for when you are ready (Key Stage 3).

pay-after-discount.title: 20% off
pay-after-discount.prompt: A football costs £80 and has 20% {{term:discount}}. The bar is the full price (100%) in 10 parts. First predict what percentage of the price you pay. Then shade the part you pay.
pay-after-discount.hint: Each part is 10%. The discount is 2 parts. You pay the rest.
pay-after-discount.success: Well done! You pay 80% of the price. Each part is £8, so 8 parts is £64.
pay-after-discount.why: How many pounds is the discount? Why are there two ways to work out the new price?
pay-after-discount.model: The discount is 2 parts: 2 × £8 = £16. One way: take the discount off the price, £80 − £16 = £64. Another way: work out 80% of the price straight away, 8 × £8 = £64. They match, because 100% − 20% = 80%.

feedback.too-small: If you shaded 2 parts, that's the discount: the money you don't pay. Shade the part you do pay.
feedback.too-big: Too much. With a discount you pay less than the full price.
feedback.empty: Nothing is shaded yet. Shade the parts you pay.

sale-price.title: The sale price
sale-price.prompt: A bike costs £240. In the sale it has 25% off. The bar is the full price in 4 parts. Predict first. Then type the sale price in pounds.
sale-price.hint: 25% is {{frac:1/4}}. How many pounds is each part? How many parts do you pay?
sale-price.success: Correct! Each part is £240 ÷ 4 = £60. You pay 3 parts: £180.
sale-price.why: Ali says "25% off means £25 cheaper". Why is he wrong?
sale-price.model: 25% means 25 in every 100, which is {{frac:1/4}} of the price, not £25. For a £240 bike, {{frac:1/4}} of the price is £60. The more something costs, the more money 25% of it is.

feedback.gave-discount: £60 is the discount. What is the new price?
feedback.minus-25: You took 25 off the price. But 25% means {{frac:1/4}} of the price, not £25.
feedback.added: You added the discount. A discount makes the price smaller.
feedback.too-big: Too much. You pay 3 of the 4 parts.
feedback.too-small: Too little. Only 1 part is the discount; you pay 3 parts.
feedback.empty: Type a number: how many pounds?

profit-percent.title: Percentage profit
profit-percent.prompt: A bike shop buys a bike for £500 and sells it for £600. The first bar is the cost (100%), and each part is 20%. Shade the profit on the second bar. First predict: what is the percentage profit?
profit-percent.hint: Each part is £100. How many pounds is the profit? How many parts?
profit-percent.success: Well done! The profit is £100, which is 1 of the 5 parts of the cost: {{frac:1/5}} = 20%. The selling price is 120% of the cost.
profit-percent.why: Another seller buys a bag for £200 and sells it for £300. That's also £100 profit. Is it also 20% profit?
profit-percent.model: No. That profit is £100 out of £200, which is {{frac:1/2}} of the cost, or 50%. The bike shop's profit was £100 out of £500, which is 20%. The money is the same, but the percentage depends on the cost. Percentage profit tells you how much was gained for every £100 spent.

feedback.sale-percent: 120% is the selling price compared with the cost. The profit is only the extra part.
feedback.wrote-money: £100 is the profit in money. What percentage of the cost is it?
feedback.too-big: Too big. The profit is only 1 of the 5 parts of the cost.
feedback.too-small: Too small. What percentage is each of the 5 parts?

loss-percent.title: Percentage loss
loss-percent.prompt: A seller bought a watch for £500 but had to sell it for £400. The bar is the cost. Tap the part that was lost so it is no longer shaded. First predict: what is the percentage loss?
loss-percent.hint: The loss is £100. How many of the 5 parts of the cost is that?
loss-percent.success: Correct! The loss is {{frac:1/5}} of the cost: 20%.
loss-percent.why: Sara worked out "100 out of 400 is 25%". Why do we use £500, not £400, for the percentage loss?
loss-percent.model: Percentage profit and loss are always compared with the cost: the money the seller spent at the start, £500. The loss is 100 out of 500: {{frac:100/500}} = {{frac:1/5}} = 20%. Sara compared it with the selling price, which only exists after the loss.

feedback.of-sale-price: You compared the loss with £400, the selling price. Use the cost (£500).
feedback.sale-percent: 80% is the selling price compared with the cost. What percentage is the loss?
feedback.wrote-money: £100 is the loss in money. What percentage of the cost is it?
feedback.too-big: Too big. The loss is only 1 of the 5 parts.
feedback.too-small: Too small. Each of the 5 parts is 20%.
